warmup.q: val crate: MutableList<Apple> = mutableListOf(Apple("Gala")), where Apple implements Fruit. Which of these lines compiles?
options: val a: MutableList<Fruit> = crate, because Apple is a subtype of Fruit
Neither: generics never allow a different type argument
warmup.why: MutableList is invariant: if MutableList<Apple> were a MutableList<Fruit>, you could add a Lemon to the crate of apples through it. Read-only List has no add, so reading apples as Fruit is always safe, and Kotlin declares it List<out E>.

opening:
The shop's apples arrive in a crate labeled "apples". A helper needs a crate of fruit to carry to the front, and the apple crate seems fine: every apple is a fruit. But the helper was told the crate holds fruit, so they top it up with a lemon. The next customer who reaches in for an apple bites into a lemon.

Kotlin refuses that hand-over in code. A MutableList<String> won't pass as a MutableList<Any>, although every String is an Any, and Java refuses the same for List<String> and List<Object>. Most people's first reaction is that the compiler is being fussy. It isn't.

Bounds and constraints wrote T : Fruit and read it as "Fruit or a subtype", without saying exactly what a subtype is. In this lesson, we'll pull classes and types apart and run the test the compiler runs on every assignment. Then we'll see what Java arrays do when they skip it, and why a read-only List<String> is a List<Any> after all. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a crate of apples and a helper who topped it up with a lemon. The compiler ran the substitution test and said no: a list you can write to must match its type exactly. Java's arrays said yes and posted a guard on every store. The read-only display case passes as a display of fruit, because nothing can go in.

Now search your code for as MutableList< or @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") near a list. Each one is a crate relabeled by hand. If the function on the other side only reads, give it a List.

Next, we'll write the promise ourselves. What must a class of your own promise before a Dispenser<Apple> may stand in for a Dispenser<Fruit>?

sections.h: One class, many types: why a class is not a type
sections.html:
Start with two words that sound alike. A class is code: a declaration such as String or ArrayList that exists at run time, and that the JVM, the program that runs your code, loads. A type is what the compiler checks: it says which values a variable may hold, and which calls are allowed on it.

Every class gives you at least two types, the plain one and the nullable one. A generic class gives you as many types as there are type arguments, the real types you fill its blank with: List<String>, List<Int>, List<Apple?>, List<List<String>>.

The two words come with two relations, and they aren't the same.

Subclassing is about classes. class Apple : Fruit means the class Apple inherits from Fruit. It's a fact about declarations.

Subtyping is about types. A type A is a subtype of B when a value of type A can be used anywhere a B is expected, and nothing can go wrong. The compiler checks that with the substitution test on every assignment and every argument: "if I secretly hand over an A where a B is expected, can any allowed move go wrong?"

Usually the two relations agree. Apple is a subclass of Fruit, and the type Apple is a subtype of the type Fruit. Here are two places where they come apart. The first exists only in Kotlin, because Java's types say nothing about null:

Java
String sure = "Fuji";
String maybe = sure;          // Java has no String?: every String may be null
String back = maybe;          // compiles, and may hand you a null later
Kotlin
val sure: String = "Fuji"
val maybe: String? = sure      // fine: String is a subtype of String?
val back: String = maybe       // error: expected 'String', actual 'String?'

There is only one class here, yet one type is a subtype of the other. A String can stand in for a String?, because a String? variable is allowed to hold a string. The reverse fails, because the value might be null.

The second place is the classic one. MutableList<String> and MutableList<Int> share a class, and the JVM can't tell them apart. ClassVsTypeDemo in the labs compares a list of variety names with a list of weights, and prints:

same runtime class:  true  (java.util.ArrayList)
MutableList::class == List::class:  true
MutableList::class.java:  interface java.util.List

Both lists are a plain java.util.ArrayList at run time. Even Kotlin's read-only List and its MutableList are one JVM interface, java.util.List. Those differences live only in the compiler. The next section shows that the compiler has a very good reason to keep them apart.

sections.h: Why a crate of apples is not a crate of fruit: invariance
sections.html:
Here is the opening's crate in code, with the shop's fruit: a Fruit interface, and Apple and Lemon as two data classes that implement it. Run the substitution test. If the compiler let you use a MutableList<Apple> where a MutableList<Fruit> is expected, could anything go wrong?

Java
List<Apple> apples = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new Apple("Gala")));
List<Fruit> anyFruit = apples;           // suppose this compiled
anyFruit.add(new Lemon("Eureka"));       // legal on a List<Fruit>
Apple second = apples.get(1);            // ClassCastException
Kotlin
val apples: MutableList<Apple> = mutableListOf(Apple("Gala"))
val anyFruit: MutableList<Fruit> = apples   // suppose this compiled
anyFruit.add(Lemon("Eureka"))                // legal on a MutableList<Fruit>
val second: Apple = apples[1]                // ClassCastException

anyFruit and apples are two names for one list object: one crate with two labels. Through the "fruit" label, you may add a lemon. Through the "apples" label, someone reads it back as an apple. So both compilers refuse the second line. javac says incompatible types: List<Apple> cannot be converted to List<Fruit>, and kotlinc says:

error: initializer type mismatch: expected 'MutableList<Fruit>', actual 'MutableList<Apple>'.

The lesson's title is the same story with the widest types there are. Swap Apple for String and Fruit for Object, and the lemon becomes an Integer: through a List<Object> view, you could add 42 to a list of strings. That is why Java won't let a List<String> pass as a List<Object>, and Kotlin won't let a MutableList<String> pass as a MutableList<Any>.

This rule is called invariance. MutableList<A> is a subtype of MutableList<B> only when A and B are the same type. It doesn't matter that Apple is a subtype of Fruit: the subtype arrow between the elements doesn't carry over to the lists. Every Java generic type is invariant in the same way.

You can force the assignment anyway, with an unchecked cast: a cast the compiler can't check, because the type argument is gone at run time. In Kotlin, apples as MutableList<Fruit> does it, with a warning: unchecked cast of 'MutableList<Apple>' to 'MutableList<Fruit>'. In Java, a cast through List<?>, a list of some unknown type, does it: (List<Fruit>) (List<?>) apples. Then the compiler does exactly what you asked. InvarianceDemo in the labs forces it and adds the lemon:

the apple crate holds 2 items, and nothing failed yet
ClassCastException: class workbench.generics.l03.demo.Lemon cannot be cast to class workbench.generics.l03.demo.Apple (...)

The lemon went in without a sound. The failure turned up later, on a read, as a ClassCastException on a line with no cast in it. It's the late failure from lesson 1 of this track, with the compiler switched off on purpose.

The crate picture breaks in one place, and it's the important one. A real crate holds its apples in plain sight, and you'd spot the lemon when you opened it. At run time, the JVM spots nothing: the list doesn't know it was meant for apples, so nothing checks the lemon until someone reads it as an apple.

A list you can write to must match its element type exactly. Don't cast your way past it.

Invariance annoys people in practice. You have a MutableList<Apple> and a function that takes a MutableList<Fruit>, and the call doesn't compile. The fix is never the cast. Ask what the function does with the list. If it only reads, it should take a read-only List<Fruit>, and the last section shows why that works. If it adds, the compiler just caught a bug: the function could have dropped a lemon into your crate of apples.

Java didn't always say no to this kind of hand-over, though. Its arrays said yes.

video.title: A crate of apples is not a crate of fruit: one list with two labels lets a lemon in, so a list you can write to must match its type exactly

sections.h: Java arrays said yes, so the JVM checks every store
sections.html:
Java made the other choice for arrays, back in Java 1.0. An Apple[] is a Fruit[], and a String[] is an Object[]:

Java
Apple[] crate = { new Apple("Gala"), new Apple("Fuji") };
Fruit[] anyFruit = crate;               // compiles: arrays are covariant
anyFruit[0] = new Lemon("Eureka");      // compiles too: a Lemon is a Fruit
// java.lang.ArrayStoreException: ...Lemon
Kotlin
val crate: Array<Apple> = arrayOf(Apple("Gala"), Apple("Fuji"))
val anyFruit: Array<Fruit> = crate
// error: initializer type mismatch: expected 'Array<Fruit>', actual 'Array<Apple>'.
val forced = crate as Array<Fruit>       // an unchecked cast gets you there...
forced[0] = Lemon("Eureka")              // ...and to the same ArrayStoreException

Arrays whose subtype arrow follows their element type, as here, are called covariant. The last section explains the word properly. This is exactly the substitution the previous section showed to be unsafe, and Java allows it anyway, then pays at run time. Every array remembers its element type, and the JVM checks every store into an array of objects. Picture a guard posted at every array, who looks at each item that goes in. When the value doesn't fit, the guard shouts: the JVM throws ArrayStoreException. ArrayStoreDemo printed:

ArrayStoreException: workbench.generics.l03.demo.ArrayStoreDemo$Lemon
crate[0] is still Gala

The guard costs a little on every store. And the error still comes at run time, maybe in a library far from the code that passed the Apple[] on as a Fruit[]. Java arrays said yes in 1996, and the JVM has checked every store ever since.

That is why the rule for generics is the way it is. An array knows its element type at run time, so the JVM can check late. A List<Apple> doesn't know its type argument at run time (lesson 8 of this track shows why), so nothing could check a late store. Java's generics had to be invariant, and so are Kotlin's.

Kotlin goes one step further and makes arrays invariant too, as its half of the snippet shows. Array<T> is a generic class like any other. So the ArrayStoreException can't happen in Kotlin code that uses Array<T>, unless you cast your way to it. If you really need to read an Array<Int> through an Array<Any> view, Kotlin has a safe way to say "read only", Array<out Any>, which lesson 6 of this track covers.

You still meet covariant arrays from Kotlin, because Java APIs pass them around. Arrays.asList, varargs and toArray all hand out arrays whose real element type may be narrower than their declared type. If a library writes into an Object[] you gave it, give it a real Object[].

So far, the answer has been "no" for lists you can write to, and "yes, with a guard" for Java arrays. There is one more answer.

try.title: Store a lemon in an apple array
steps: Run ArrayStoreDemo. Before it runs, predict whether anyFruit[0] = new Lemon("Eureka") compiles, and whether it runs.
Uncomment List<Fruit> fruitList = apples; and run again. Compare the two answers Java gives.
Run the Kotlin twin, ArrayStoreDemo.kt, then uncomment its val refused line. What did Kotlin need before it could fall into the same trap?

code.title: ArrayStoreDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.generics.l03.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** Java arrays are covariant, so the JVM must check every store. Java generics are invariant instead. */ public class ArrayStoreDemo { interface Fruit { String name(); } record Apple(String name) implements Fruit {} record Lemon(String name) implements Fruit {} public static void main(String[] args) { Apple[] crate = { new Apple("Gala"), new Apple("Fuji") }; Fruit[] anyFruit = crate; // compiles: an Apple[] is a Fruit[] try { anyFruit[0] = new Lemon("Eureka"); // compiles too: a Lemon is a Fruit System.out.println("stored a lemon"); } catch (ArrayStoreException e) { System.out.println("ArrayStoreException: " + e.getMessage()); } List<Apple> apples = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new Apple("Gala"))); // Step 2: uncomment the next line and run. javac refuses it. // List<Fruit> fruitList = apples; System.out.println("crate[0] is still " + crate[0].name()); } }

Once you do, the JVM's store check fires exactly as it does for Java. // Fruit, Apple and Lemon are the classes declared in InvarianceDemo.kt. package workbench.generics.l03.demo fun main() { val crate: Array<Apple> = arrayOf(Apple("Gala"), Apple("Fuji")) // Step 2: uncomment the next line and run. Kotlin refuses it: arrays are invariant. // val refused: Array<Fruit> = crate @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") val anyFruit = crate as Array<Fruit> // forced: at run time an Apple[] really is a Fruit[] try { anyFruit[0] = Lemon("Eureka") // compiles: a Lemon is a Fruit println("stored a lemon") } catch (e: ArrayStoreException) { println("ArrayStoreException: ${e.message}") } println("crate[0] is still ${crate[0].name}") }

The list line doesn't compile: incompatible types: List<Apple> cannot be converted to List<Fruit>. Arrays check late, generics check early. The Kotlin twin prints ArrayStoreException: workbench.generics.l03.demo.Lemon, but only after an unchecked cast. Its val refused: Array<Fruit> = crate line fails with Initializer type mismatch: expected 'Array<Fruit>', actual 'Array<Apple>'.

aside.title: Why did Java make arrays covariant at all?
aside.html: Because Java 1.0 had no generics. Without them, the only way to write one method that sorts or compares arrays of any kind of object was to take an Object[], the way Arrays.sort(Object[] a) still does. For that method to accept a String[], a String[] had to count as an Object[]. The guard on every store was the price of that convenience. When generics arrived in Java 5, type parameters could solve the same problem without a guard, as long as generic types stayed invariant.

sections.h: The display case: why a read-only List<String> is a List<Any>
sections.html:
After two sections of "no", here is a "yes" that seems to break the rule. Picture the shop window. The apples sit in a glass display case: customers can see every one of them, but there's no way to put anything in. Calling it "a display of fruit" is honest, because everything you can see in it is fruit.

Kotlin's read-only List is that display case. Java has no read-only List type, so it needs a wildcard to say the same thing: a ? in the angle brackets, which means "some type I don't name". ? extends Fruit reads as "some subtype of Fruit":

Java
List<Apple> crate = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new Apple("Gala")));
List<? extends Fruit> display = crate;   // compiles: a read-only view, written where it is used
Kotlin
val crate: MutableList<Apple> = mutableListOf(Apple("Gala"))
val display: List<Fruit> = crate        // compiles

Run the substitution test again, on the read-only List. What can a caller do with a List<Fruit>? Read items, as Fruit. Ask the size. Go through them in a loop. There is no add and no set. Every item of a List<Apple> really is a Fruit, so every read through the Fruit view tells the truth. Nothing can go wrong, so the compiler allows it.

That is the whole idea behind covariance: when a type only hands values out and never takes them in, its subtype arrow can follow the element type. Apple is a subtype of Fruit, so List<Apple> is a subtype of List<Fruit>, and List<String> is a subtype of List<Any>. Kotlin's List is declared as List<out E>, and the out is the promise that E only comes out. The next lesson is about writing that promise yourself.

Notice what display doesn't let you do. Kotlin's List has no add at all:

display.add(Lemon("Eureka"))
// error: unresolved reference 'add' on receiver of type 'List<Fruit>'.

javac rejects display.add(new Lemon("Eureka")) with Lemon cannot be converted to CAP#1. CAP#1 is javac's name for the unknown type behind the ?, and no lemon is known to fit it. The arrow also points one way only. val back: List<Apple> = display fails with expected 'List<Apple>', actual 'List<Fruit>', because a display of fruit might hold a lemon.

Here the display case picture breaks. A glass case is closed to customers, but the shopkeeper, who has the key, can still change what's inside. The list object is still the mutable crate: crate.add(Apple("Fuji")) works, and display sees the new apple. The List<Fruit> type only removes the ways to write through this reference. Read-only isn't the same as unchanging.

At run time, List and MutableList are the same java.util.List, so all of this is checked at compile time and costs nothing. Java writes List<? extends Fruit> at each use instead, and lesson 6 of this track maps those wildcards onto Kotlin.

You now have the three answers a generic type can give to "is C<Apple> a C<Fruit>?". Yes, for a type that only hands values out, like List. No, for a type you can write to, like MutableList and every Java generic. And "yes, then a guard checks every store", for Java arrays.

Here is today's limit. The compiler knows List is safe to widen only because the standard library declared it out. For a type of your own, a dispenser, say, it can't tell, so it plays safe and says no. Writing the promise is the next step.

alt.title: ReadOnlyListDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.generics.l03.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** Java twin of ReadOnlyListDemo.kt. Java has no read-only List type, so it writes the read-only view as ? extends. */ public class ReadOnlyListDemoJava { interface Fruit { String name(); } record Apple(String name) implements Fruit {} record Lemon(String name) implements Fruit {} public static void main(String[] args) { List<Apple> crate = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new Apple("Gala"))); Integer[] weights = { 180, 150 }; List<? extends Fruit> display = crate; // compiles: a read-only view, spelled at the use site System.out.println("as List<? extends Fruit>: " + display + ", first item is an " + display.get(0).getClass().getSimpleName()); // List<Fruit> anyCrate = crate; // 1 // Object[] anys = weights; // 2 // display.add(new Lemon("Eureka")); // 3 // List<Apple> back = display; // 4 System.out.println("weights: " + weights[0] + ", " + weights[1]); } }

try.expect: The demo itself prints as List<Fruit>: [Apple(name=Gala)], first item is an Apple. All four lines fail. 1: expected 'MutableList<Fruit>', actual 'MutableList<Apple>' (invariant). 2: expected 'Array<Any>', actual 'Array<Int>' (Kotlin arrays are invariant). 3: Unresolved reference 'add' on receiver of type 'List<Fruit>' (read-only). 4: expected 'List<Apple>', actual 'List<Fruit>': covariance goes up the arrow, never down. The Java twin differs on line 2 only: Object[] anys = weights compiles, because Java arrays are covariant. Lines 3 and 4 fail with Lemon cannot be converted to CAP#1 and List<CAP#1> cannot be converted to List<Apple>.

compare.title: Invariance and arrays in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Variance.java
java.html: import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; class Variance { static void demo() { List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(); // List<Object> objects = names; // error: invariant List<? extends Object> view = names; // OK: a read-only view, written at the use site Object first = view.isEmpty() ? null : view.get(0); String[] varieties = { "Gala" }; Object[] objects = varieties; // OK: arrays are covariant objects[0] = 42; // compiles, throws ArrayStoreException } }

kotlin.title: Variance.kt
kotlin.html: fun demo() { val names: MutableList<String> = mutableListOf() // val objects: MutableList<Any> = names // error: invariant val view: List<Any> = names // OK: List is declared List<out E> val first: Any? = view.firstOrNull() val varieties: Array<String> = arrayOf("Gala") // val objects: Array<Any> = varieties // error: Kotlin arrays are invariant val readOnly: Array<out Any> = varieties // OK: you can read, not write }

compare.note: Both languages make generic types invariant, for the same reason: the type argument is gone at run time, so a bad write could not be caught later. The differences are in the exceptions to that rule. Java made arrays covariant and checks each store at run time. Kotlin makes arrays invariant like everything else. For the safe read-only case, Java asks you to write a wildcard (List<? extends Object>) at every use, while Kotlin's List declares out once, so a plain List<Any> parameter already accepts a List<String>. Kotlin's List and MutableList are the same java.util.List at run time; the split exists only for the compiler.

worked.title: Why a crate of apples won't go into addFreeLemon

steps.say: Every order that leaves the shop gets a free lemon on top, and a shared helper adds it. A caller has a crate of apples, and the call doesn't compile. Before reading on, run the substitution test yourself: what could the helper do to the caller's crate?
steps.code: interface Fruit { val grams: Int } data class Apple(override val grams: Int) : Fruit data class Lemon(override val grams: Int) : Fruit fun addFreeLemon(order: MutableList<Fruit>) { order.add(Lemon(100)) } val apples: MutableList<Apple> = mutableListOf(Apple(180)) addFreeLemon(apples) // error: argument type mismatch: actual type is 'MutableList<Apple>', // but 'MutableList<Fruit>' was expected.

alt.html: interface Fruit { int grams(); } record Apple(int grams) implements Fruit {} record Lemon(int grams) implements Fruit {} static void addFreeLemon(List<Fruit> order) { order.add(new Lemon(100)); } List<Apple> apples = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new Apple(180))); addFreeLemon(apples); // error: incompatible types: List<Apple> cannot be converted to List<Fruit>

steps.say: 1. Imagine it compiled. The helper drops a Lemon into the caller's crate. The caller later reads apples[1] as an Apple, and gets a ClassCastException. The compiler's "no" was right, and an unchecked cast would only hide it.

1. Split reading from writing. Weighing the order only reads, so that part takes a read-only List<Fruit> (Java: List<? extends Fruit>), which accepts the crate of apples. Adding the lemon needs a list that is allowed to hold any fruit, so the caller builds one: a bag for the whole order.
steps.code: fun weightOf(order: List<Fruit>): Int = order.sumOf { it.grams } val weight = weightOf(apples) // compiles: List is covariant val bag: MutableList<Fruit> = mutableListOf() bag.addAll(apples) addFreeLemon(bag) // a list that may hold any fruit

alt.html: static int weightOf(List<? extends Fruit> order) { return order.stream().mapToInt(Fruit::grams).sum(); } int weight = weightOf(apples); // compiles: ? extends makes it a read-only view List<Fruit> bag = new ArrayList<>(); bag.addAll(apples); addFreeLemon(bag);

steps.say: 1. Check the result against the figure's arrows, with Apple and Fruit in place of String and Any. MutableList<Apple> points to List<Apple>, which points to List<Fruit>. Every arrow is a read-only one. The only list that receives a lemon is declared to hold any Fruit.

lab.title: Build a tiny subtype checker, then tame Java arrays
steps: Run the tests once. All eleven fail. Read the small world of classes at the top of SubtypingTest: it wires String, Fruit, Apple, List, MutableList and ArrayList the way Kotlin does, with List marked covariant.
In TypeModel.kt, write isSubclass: the same class, or any of sub.supers is a subclass of sup. It only needs recursion, a function that calls itself.
Write isSubtype with the three rules from its KDoc, in order: nullability, then classes, then type arguments. Use sup.klass.covariant to pick between "subtype" and "equal" for each argument.
Run the Kotlin tests. If the nested test fails, check that your covariant branch calls isSubtype again rather than comparing classes.
In ArrayChecks.java, write canStore by asking the array for its element type, array.getClass().getComponentType(), and write widenSafely with Arrays.copyOf(names, names.length, Object[].class).
Run the tests until all eleven pass.
hints: isSubclass(sub, sup) = sub === sup || sub.supers.any { isSubclass(it, sup) }.
For each i in sup.args.indices, compare sub.args[i] with sup.args[i]. Type is a data class, so == compares structure.
Class.isInstance(value) is the reflective form of Java's instanceof.
lab.done: All seven tests in SubtypingTest and all four in ArrayChecksTest pass.

drill.title: Run the substitution test from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. On paper, write the four-line snippet that shows why MutableList<String> must not be a MutableList<Any>: declare the list, assign it to the wider type, add a wrong value, read it back. Mark the line the compiler rejects and the line that would throw. Then write the same four lines in Java with List<String>, and the Java array version, and mark where each one throws.

answer.html: val varieties: MutableList<String> = mutableListOf("Gala") val anything: MutableList<Any> = varieties // rejected: MutableList is invariant anything.add(42) // would be legal on MutableList<Any> val second: String = varieties[1] // would throw ClassCastException // Java arrays: compiles, fails at the store // String[] names = { "Gala" }; // Object[] objects = names; // allowed: arrays are covariant // objects[0] = 42; // ArrayStoreException here

alt.title: Substitution.java
alt.html: List<String> varieties = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Gala")); List<Object> anything = varieties; // rejected: Java generics are invariant anything.add(42); // would be legal on List<Object> String second = varieties.get(1); // would throw ClassCastException // arrays: compiles, fails at the store String[] names = { "Gala" }; Object[] objects = names; // allowed: arrays are covariant objects[0] = 42; // ArrayStoreException here

recap: A class is a declaration that exists at run time. A type is what the compiler checks. One class gives many types: String and String?, List<String> and List<Int>.
A is a subtype of B when an A can be used anywhere a B is expected without anything going wrong: the substitution test.

A MutableList<Apple> is not a MutableList<Fruit>, and a Java List<String> is not a List<Object>: through the wider type you could add a lemon, or an Integer. Generic types you can write to are invariant, in Java and Kotlin, and an unchecked cast only moves the failure to a later read.
Java arrays are covariant and pay for it with a run-time check on every store (ArrayStoreException). Kotlin's Array<T> is invariant.
A read-only List<Apple> is a List<Fruit>, because a list you can only read can't receive a wrong value. Kotlin declares this with List<out E>, and Java spells it List<? extends Fruit> at each use.
The limit: the compiler widens List only because the library declared it out. For your own generic types, it says no until you make the same promise.

explain.prompt: A colleague asks: "String is a subtype of Any, so why won't Kotlin let me pass my MutableList<String> to a function that takes MutableList<Any>? And why does it accept a List<Any>?" Explain it in your own words.
explain.answer: The compiler checks whether one type can safely stand in for another. A function that takes MutableList<Any> is allowed to add anything, say an Int. If you could pass your MutableList<String>, the Int would end up in your list of strings, like a lemon dropped into a crate of apples, and your next read would throw a ClassCastException. So mutable generic types are invariant: the type arguments must match exactly. A read-only List<Any> has no way to add. The function can only read, and every element of your list really is an Any, so passing a List<String> is safe. Kotlin marks this with out on List. Java arrays allow the unsafe version and check every store at run time instead.

deeper.html:
Why could Java afford covariant arrays but not covariant generics? Arrays are reified: every array object carries its element type, so the JVM can check each store. Generic types are erased: an ArrayList<String> is just an ArrayList at run time, so no check is possible after compilation. Lesson 8 of this track is about erasure.

Array covariance is also why Java has the odd "generic array creation" error. new List<String>[10] is rejected, because the array would remember only List, and its store check could not stop a List<Integer> from going in.

In the lab's toy model, a generic class hands its arguments straight to its supertypes. Real Kotlin is more flexible: class StringMap<V> : HashMap<String, V>() fixes one argument and passes the other, and the compiler tracks that mapping for every supertype. The rules in the lab still hold; the real checker just does more bookkeeping.

One more pair to keep apart: Nothing is a subtype of every type, and Any? is a supertype of every type. Lesson 10 of this track uses Nothing to explain why emptyList() fits every List<T>.
